flashcards.q: What is the AAA triad and what does each A answer?
flashcards.a: Authentication (who are you) -> Authorization (what can you do, on what resource) -> Accounting (what actually happened). Three separate concerns with three separate failure modes.

flashcards.q: What is the architectural rule for where authentication and authorization should each happen?
flashcards.a: Authenticate ONCE at the edge (produce a trusted identity token); authorize AT THE RESOURCE, on every action, every time -- never assume a valid token implies a permitted action.

flashcards.q: What is the root cause of most BOLA/IDOR vulnerabilities?
flashcards.a: An authorization check that verifies scope/route-level permission (can this identity read orders in general) but never checks object-level ownership (does this specific order belong to this specific caller).

flashcards.q: What's the difference between HTTP 401 and 403?
flashcards.a: 401 Unauthorized = authentication failed or missing (server doesn't know who you are). 403 Forbidden = authentication succeeded but authorization denied the specific action.

flashcards.q: Name the three authorization models and their key tradeoff.
flashcards.a: RBAC (role->permissions, cheap, breaks down at per-object sharing = role explosion); ABAC (policy over attributes, expressive, hard to audit exhaustively); ReBAC (graph of typed relationships, Zanzibar-style, answers per-object sharing questions RBAC can't).

flashcards.q: What is role explosion and how do you detect it in an unfamiliar codebase?
flashcards.a: Minting a role per object instead of per business function (e.g. editor_of_doc_123) to fake per-object sharing with RBAC. Detect by checking if role count grows with object/resource count rather than staying a small stable set.

flashcards.q: What latency and scale does Google's Zanzibar authorization system achieve in production?
flashcards.a: Sub-10ms p95 latency, trillions of ACL/relationship tuples, millions of authorization requests per second. OSS implementations (OpenFGA, SpiceDB, Ory Keto) report production FGA query latency of 1-10ms.

flashcards.q: What are the three required properties of a real accounting/audit system, versus scattered log statements?
flashcards.a: 1) Both allows AND denies are logged, not just denials. 2) The log is append-only, tamper-evident, and centralized, not ephemeral stdout. 3) Each entry records who/what/when/from-where/decision AND the policy version in effect at that time.

flashcards.q: Why is accounting usually the weakest of the three A's in production systems?
flashcards.a: It has no immediate functional payoff -- nothing visibly breaks if it's missing -- until an incident, at which point its absence is catastrophic. Median breach dwell time in industry reports is measured in months, almost always an accounting/alerting failure rather than an authn/authz one.

flashcards.q: What 2026 passkey/FIDO2 adoption numbers should you know?
flashcards.a: ~5 billion active passkeys worldwide, 75% of consumers have enabled one on at least one account, ~48% of the world's top 100 websites support passkeys, and passkeys see a 93% authentication success rate vs 63% for traditional methods.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't fine-grained permissions be baked directly into a JWT's claims?
flashcards.a: Coarse, slow-changing claims (role, tenant ID) are fine to embed since a short TTL bounds staleness, but fine-grained fast-changing permissions embedded in the token mean a permission revocation doesn't take effect until the token expires -- the token itself becomes stale authorization state.

flashcards.q: For an LLM agent calling tools on a user's behalf, what authorization pattern applies?
flashcards.a: The agent gets its own scoped, short-lived, delegated identity carrying the MINIMUM permissions for the current task (not the user's full permission set). Each tool call is authorized independently at execution time, not once at agent-start, and irreversible/sensitive actions should trigger a fresh step-up check.
